read: full: main text pp. 1-9 and appendices A.1, A.3, A.4, B.3-B.6 and D (pp. 13-22) read in full; template code (A.2), annotation platform (B.2), model table (C), extra results (E) and error examples (F) skimmed
venue_now: arXiv v4, 30 Apr 2026 (p. 1); no venue header in this text, though it thanks anonymous reviewers (p. 9); papers.json records ACL 2026 (Long Papers), pp. 14529-14553
what_it_is: FinChain is a symbolic benchmark for verifiable chain-of-thought reasoning in finance. Following GSM-Symbolic, it builds 290 parameterised templates over 58 topics in 12 financial domains, with two basic, two intermediate and one advanced template per topic. Each template is an executable Python program that generates a question together with a gold step-by-step solution and its intermediate results (pp. 1-4). Templates were drafted with LLM assistance, checked by automatic validation rules and reviewed by financial experts (pp. 4, 13-17). Its metric, ChainEval, aligns a model's steps with the gold chain by dynamic time warping. Each step pair is scored by sentence-encoder similarity gated by a 5% match of the intermediate result, and final-answer correctness is added (pp. 4-5). 26 LLMs were evaluated on 2,900 instances, 10 per template (pp. 5-6).
domain: finance: 12 domains, 58 topics (e.g. corporate finance, investment analysis, risk management, crypto finance) (Figure 2, p. 3)
size: 290 templates (116 basic, 116 intermediate, 58 advanced; mean gold steps 2.01, 2.97 and 3.90), 2,900 evaluated instances, 26 LLMs (pp. 4-6)
source_of_items: generated from templates: executable Python templates drafted with LLM assistance from a prompt modelled on GSM-Symbolic, then validated and curated by financial experts (pp. 3-4, 13-15)
has_gold_traces: yes: every instance comes with an executable gold chain of steps and intermediate values computed by the template (pp. 2-3; Figure 1, p. 1)
evaluation: step-level (process). ChainEval = 0.9 x a DTW alignment score over step pairs + 0.1 x final-answer correctness (FAC). Each step pair scores sentence-encoder cosine similarity times an indicator that the intermediate result is within 5% relative tolerance; FAC uses the same tolerance (pp. 4-5). Steps are parsed by regular expressions, with an LLM parser as fallback (pp. 7, 21-22). ROUGE-2, ROUGE-L and BERTScore are reported for comparison (p. 7)
human_validation: Templates: ten financial experts (seven graduate students, three industry professionals) took part. After a 20-template calibration pilot reviewed by all of them, the other 270 templates were reviewed by one expert each. 29 of 290 (10%) were found incorrect and revised (pp. 4, 15, 17). Metric: experts rated 100 responses (20 questions x 5 models) on 1-5 scales for reasoning-process quality and final-answer accuracy (pp. 5-6, 17-18). ChainEval correlates with the process ratings at Spearman 0.655 (Pearson 0.584, Kendall 0.509), against ROUGE-2 0.469, ROUGE-L 0.434 and BERTScore 0.287 (pp. 20-21). No inter-annotator agreement is reported, and the weights alpha and epsilon were chosen to maximise correlation with these same ratings (pp. 5, 20-21). Error labels on 200 sampled questions were checked by experts (p. 8).
contamination_measures: generated instances; the paper calls its generation 'contamination-free' (pp. 1-2, 9), but templates and code are released under the MIT licence (p. 9), and there is no private split

engtrace_use.sentence: S-I2 (L84-94): 'Symbolic templates (Mirzadeh et al., 2024; Xie et al., 2025) serve as the generative mechanism, producing unique, contamination-resistant instances'
engtrace_use.explanation: Taken alone, S-I2 is accurate. FinChain does generate unique instances from parameterised templates (pp. 2-3) and calls the generation contamination-free (p. 1). But by citing FinChain only for that mechanism, the May text omits what matters most for the comparison, and the protocol counts that as misleading. FinChain already pairs every generated instance with an executable gold chain of thought (p. 2), already scores model steps against that chain (ChainEval, pp. 4-5), and validates the metric against expert ratings (pp. 5-6, 20). Meanwhile, the sentence just before S-I2 (L81-83), contribution 1 and the Related Work closing (S-E3, L201-205) present 'a symbolic benchmark that pairs unique problem instances with gold-standard reasoning traces to enable verifiable process supervision' as what EngTrace introduces. The claim at L77-80 is scoped to engineering, so FinChain does not falsify it. S-E3's unqualified 'existing benchmarks remain limited to outcome matching', however, is contradicted by FinChain unless it is restricted to engineering.

suggested_wording: The closest precedent is FinChain (Xie et al., 2025), whose 290 executable templates for financial reasoning generate each question with a gold chain of intermediate computations; its ChainEval metric aligns a model's steps with that chain, scoring embedding similarity gated by a 5% match of each intermediate result, and adds final-answer correctness.
facts_to_cite: A symbolic benchmark for verifiable chain-of-thought financial reasoning: 58 topics across 12 domains, five templates per topic (two basic, two intermediate, one advanced), 290 templates in all (pp. 1-4)
Templates follow GSM-Symbolic (Mirzadeh et al.) and are executable Python programs that generate the question, the gold intermediate steps and the final answer (pp. 2-3)
Mean gold steps: 2.01 basic, 2.97 intermediate, 3.90 advanced (Table 1, p. 4)

Templates were drafted with LLM assistance; ten financial experts reviewed them, one expert per template after a 20-template calibration pilot, and 29 of 290 were found incorrect and revised (pp. 4, 15, 17)
Every template requires a single target value (p. 15)
Evaluation set: 10 instances per template, 2,900 test cases; 26 LLMs evaluated zero-shot, one of them (Grok-4 Heavy) only on a 200-instance subset (pp. 5-7)

ChainEval: DTW alignment of predicted and gold steps, each pair scored by sentence-encoder similarity times a 5%-tolerance match of the intermediate result, combined with final-answer correctness at weight 0.1 (pp. 4-5)
On 100 responses, ChainEval correlates with expert ratings of reasoning-process quality at Spearman 0.655, against 0.469 for ROUGE-2 and 0.287 for BERTScore (pp. 5-6; Table 5, p. 20)
For some reasoning models final-answer correctness and ChainEval diverge, so correct final answers do not guarantee faithful intermediate steps (p. 7)
The paper describes its generation as contamination-free (p. 1) and releases data and code under the MIT licence (p. 9)
Its stated limitation: the items are entirely synthetic and may lack the linguistic diversity of real financial text (p. 9)
overlap_with_engtrace: Shares nearly the whole design: symbolic templates that generate instances; executable gold traces with intermediate values; a three-tier difficulty split; step-level scoring against the gold; expert review of templates; expert validation of the metric, with ROUGE and BERTScore as foils; and the synthetic-language limitation. Differs, on the EngTrace side as described in the state brief, in five ways. (1) Domain: engineering, with unit-bearing quantities and multipart, vector, array, symbolic and classification answers, where FinChain requires a single target (p. 15). (2) Step checks: EngTrace's are mostly deterministic (order-free milestone matching at 0.5%, recomputation of displayed arithmetic) with a residual LLM judge, where ChainEval uses embedding similarity and order-preserving DTW at 5% (pp. 4-5). (3) Validation: EngTrace reports inter-rater agreement (three own-branch experts per trace on 300 traces), trace-level AUROC and planted defects, where FinChain reports a correlation on 100 responses, with parameters tuned on the same ratings and no agreement statistic (pp. 5, 20-21). (4) Templates: three-expert certification with planted defects, against one expert per template (p. 15). (5) Pool: a private seed and hashed pool, against public MIT-licensed templates (p. 9).
notes: Shared authorship: the citation map lists four EngTrace authors on FinChain (Zhuohan Xie, Fan Zhang, Veselin Stoyanov, Preslav Nakov; p. 1). The revised text must discuss FinChain in the third person, for ARR anonymity, and should expect reviewers to compare the two closely. That is why what EngTrace adds must be stated beyond the change of domain (see overlap). The May paper's old validation (Tribunal rho = 0.632 against NLP metrics at 0.325, contribution 2) mirrors FinChain's design (ChainEval 0.655 against ROUGE and BERTScore); the revised paper's expert-agreement validation is the methodological difference to stress. For Batch G: FinChain's first sentence (p. 1) cites '(Zhao et al., 2023; Xie et al., 2023b)', with Xie 2023b being the storytelling study (p. 12). That is the pair the May S-I1 cites, for a different claim. FinChain also cites DeltaScore (Xie et al., 2023c) for ROUGE and BERTScore as reference-based measures (p. 7), as the May S-T does. The May reference lacks the arXiv id 2506.02515 (citation map D.3). The text reviewed is v4 (30 Apr 2026), so the 26-model results and some validation details may postdate the version the May authors read.
